body.heading: Magnetism with a switch
paragraphs: Pass an electric current through a wire and a magnetic field appears around it. Wind the wire into a coil and the fields of the loops add together, concentrating into a strong field along the coil's axis — one end behaves as a north pole, the other as a south. Add an iron core and the effect multiplies, as the iron itself becomes magnetised and joins in.

The defining feature is control. Switch the current on and the magnet exists; switch it off and the magnetism vanishes almost completely. Reverse the current and the poles swap ends. No permanent magnet offers any of that.

body.heading: Turning the strength up and down
paragraphs: An electromagnet's strength is adjustable in ways a bar magnet's never can be. More turns of wire in the coil, a larger current, or a better iron core all make it stronger. Engineers dial in exactly the magnetism a job needs, from the faint pull in a doorbell to forces that lift cars.

That doorbell is a neat demonstration: press the button and current flows, the electromagnet yanks a hammer against the bell, the movement breaks the circuit, the magnetism dies, a spring pulls the hammer back — and the circuit reconnects to repeat the cycle dozens of times a second.

body.heading: The electromagnet at large
paragraphs: Scrapyards use electromagnets as cranes: lower the magnet onto a wrecked car, switch on, lift; position it over the truck, switch off, and the car drops. A permanent magnet that strong would be useless — nothing could ever be unloaded from it.

The same principle spins every electric motor, opens and closes countless valves and relays, and — in superconducting form, cooled until resistance vanishes — generates the immense steady fields inside MRI scanners. Magnetism you can switch is one of the foundation technologies of the modern world.

description: A coil of wire and a current make a magnet you can switch, strengthen and reverse — the trick behind cranes, motors and MRI scanners.
